brief:
Yasser Abbas holds three positions no election of the Palestinian public gave him: a seat on Fatah's Central Committee, his father's mandate over the PLO's properties in Lebanon, and — if reports this newspaper has not been able to confirm hold true — the leadership of a company being formed to centralise the West Bank's fuel purchasing. He is also, and has been for two decades, a businessman whose markets sit inside the territory his father governs.

This report assembles the published record of that career: the contracts, the scrutiny, the court case he brought and lost, and the new mandates of the past eighteen months. It is a record of documents, not accusations. Where the record establishes a fact, this report states it; where it establishes only a question, this report says so — and notes that no court has ever convicted Yasser Abbas, or any member of his family, of any crime.

## The companies

The business core is Falcon Holding Group, the conglomerate Yasser Abbas chairs. Its engineering arm, the Falcon Electrical Mechanical Contracting Company, was established in 2000 — the year his father's predecessor was besieged in Ramallah — and grew offices in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Qatar and the Emirates. Foreign Policy's 2012 investigation reported that another arm, Falcon Tobacco, held the monopoly on US-made cigarettes in the Palestinian territories.

American taxpayers appear in the ledger too. The engineering company received $1.89 million from USAID in 2005 to build a sewage network in Hebron, and a second family firm, First Option Project Construction Management, received some $300,000 more — figures reported by Foreign Policy and entered into the US congressional record. Reuters had begun tying the president's sons to deals carrying US taxpayer support as early as 2009.

None of this was hidden, and none of it was illegal. The question it raised was structural, and it is the question that has followed him since: whether a market can be fair when one competitor's father appoints the regulators, the licensers and the judges.

## Washington asks the question

In July 2012 the US House subcommittee on the Middle East held a hearing under a blunt title: "Chronic Kleptocracy: Corruption within the Palestinian Political Establishment." Congressman Steve Chabot charged that the president had used his position to enrich himself and his sons; the former White House official Elliott Abrams testified that corruption was destroying "faith in the entire political system." The Palestinian leadership dismissed the hearing as politically motivated, as Haaretz reported at the time.

The hearing convicted no one, and its allegations remain allegations. What it fixed in the official record of Washington — the Authority's largest Western patron at the time — was that the family's business standing had become a matter of US oversight interest.

## He sued, and the courts kept the question open

Foreign Policy's investigation was built around two questions, and Yasser Abbas went to federal court in Washington to make them unaskable:

> Are the sons of the Palestinian president growing rich off their father's system? Have they enriched themselves at the expense of regular Palestinians — and even US taxpayers?
> Foreign Policy, "The Brothers Abbas", June 2012 — the questions Yasser Abbas sued over

He lost. A federal judge dismissed his libel suit in 2013, and the DC Circuit affirmed in 2015, in an opinion by then-Judge Brett Kavanaugh: the questions were questions, not false statements of fact, and a free press may ask them. Abbas maintained throughout that the insinuations were false and that his companies won their work on merit. The courts did not rule on who was right — they ruled the asking lawful. That distinction is this report's own method.

## The new mandates

For a decade the file was quiet. Then, in 2025, President Abbas sent his son to Beirut to oversee the sale of the PLO's land and properties in Lebanon — a mandate over national assets, reported by Asharq Al-Awsat, that no representative body reviewed. The sitting ambassador, Ashraf Dabbour, was dismissed; in April he publicly accused Yasser Abbas of turning the security services on him; on Monday, Lebanon [arrested Dabbour on a Ramallah warrant](https://www.timesofpalestine.com/en/story/eb10f3b698.html) for extradition on embezzlement charges he denies.

In May, Yasser Abbas entered Fatah's Central Committee on his first run, eighth of eighteen, as [our congress deep dive](https://www.timesofpalestine.com/en/story/4fb4204cb0.html) reported — his first formal political rank. And in the West Bank's fuel crisis, Palestinian outlets now report — without official confirmation, and this newspaper repeats the caveat — that a new centralised fuel-purchasing company is being prepared under his leadership, while the sector's biggest private operator sits in detention.

## The household

The record extends past one son. Reporting cited in the congressional record described his brother Tarek Abbas, who ran the family's advertising and communications interests, as a multimillionaire with property in Amman, Beirut and London. The president's own declared salary has never explained the family's standing, a gap the 2012 hearing pressed without resolving. The family has never published an accounting that would close the question, and no Palestinian institution has compelled one.

That last clause is the finding. The Authority's president has governed without a parliament since 2007; [every security service answers to his decree](https://www.timesofpalestine.com/en/story/906aa59f99.html); no audit body his office does not control has ever examined the family's interests. A business career conducted entirely inside that system may be honest — but no institution exists that could establish it, and that absence, not any single contract, is what two decades of documents describe.

This newspaper now maintains the Yasser Abbas file as a standing beat: the Lebanon property sales, the fuel sector, and every financial mandate that follows will be reported as the record develops, in both languages, with the same rule applied here — the documents speak, and the gaps are named.
